issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' is hard to reconcile with a stalking trauma in the absence of any indication that other people died or were put at comparable lethal risk. For this trauma type, that appraisal is clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste trigger is not impossible, but for stalking it lacks support from the rest of the profile: there are no memory items or contextual details suggesting an event involving gustatory cues. Given the formulation also has no Triggers ↔ Memory linkage, this trigger is clinically unsupported and difficult to explain in this profile.

vignette: It began on a Tuesday in November, when Elias, then twenty-nine, noticed the same dark sedan idling outside his tutoring studio after hours. Within weeks, the car was replaced by a rider on a loud motorcycle who began circling the block every evening, sometimes rolling down the window just enough to speak. The man never raised his voice. He spoke in a steady, measured tone, laying out grievances about a student’s progress and implying exactly what would happen if Elias ignored his demands. Elias had come to believe that the quietest voices carried the most lethal intent. He stopped leaving his building after six. He checked the peephole three times before answering the door. When the motorcycle engine finally cut out outside his apartment, he would sit on the floor with his back to the wall, waiting for the handle to turn. The constant sensation of being tracked became a quiet hum beneath his skin. By spring, the routine had hardened into something unbreakable. Sleep became fractured. He found himself lying awake, counting the breaths between distant car doors, his mind fixed on the possibility that the motorcycle would return. When he finally drifted off, he woke gasping as the hum of the refrigerator sounded like a distant engine. He caught himself gripping the steering wheel whenever a rider passed on the highway, his heart hammering as if the brakes were failing. His body often reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. In the library where he usually met students, he would scan the stacks for shadows, certain that someone was mapping his movements, yet when he turned, there was only the quiet rustle of turning pages. His work as a tutor required careful navigation. He avoided going to unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger. If a client suggested a new location, he would politely decline, explaining that he only worked from his designated home office or the familiar study at the public library. The library became both sanctuary and trigger. During sessions, he kept his chair angled toward the door, his eyes constantly tracking the motorcycle parked in the street below. When the engine revved, he would abruptly close the textbook, excuse himself to the restroom, and count the seconds until the sound faded. He told himself he deserved to suffer. He had come to believe he couldn’t trust his judgment. He avoided relaxing; it felt dangerous. He convinced himself that people were not what they seemed, and that people simply couldn’t be trusted. His marriage, once filled with easy laughter, grew quiet. Clara kept asking if he was sleeping, if he wanted to go to the movies, if he still trusted her. Elias loved her, but being emotionally close or intimate with others felt like leaving a door unlocked. He stopped answering her questions about his day. He stopped letting her touch his shoulder when she passed. At thirty-two, Elias walked into a community health clinic with a referral slip from his primary care doctor. He had spent months telling himself that endurance was the only proof of safety, but the false alarms no longer felt like vigilance; they felt like a prison. He was hoping someone could teach him how to stop bracing for an impact that might never come, though he was most afraid that if he ever truly relaxed, he would hear the engine again, and this time he would be too slow to react.
